output.text_response:
Here is the research-plan agent's full response:

---

**Mode: create** — no prior plans existed for q_001 ("Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?").

**Facts already recorded in the tree that bear on q_001:**
- Patrick Flynn (I1): Birth ~1845, Ireland (S1, 1850 Census, dwelling 84) — the objective states Pennsylvania, but the 1850 census says Ireland; the discrepancy is unresolved.
- Patrick Flynn (I1): Death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (S3, death cert. no. 4521) — in tree; no parental-information assertions extracted from it for q_001 yet.
- Thomas Flynn (I2): Birth ~1818, Ireland — fact in tree, no source attached.
- ParentChild Thomas→Patrick (R1): supported by S1, S2, S3 — all indirect; no direct parentage evidence yet.
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records): in the project, but no assertions extracted for q_001.
- **No mother is named anywhere in the tree.**

---

**Plan pl_002 — 9 items:**

| # | Step | Record Set | Repository | Notes |
|---|------|-----------|------------|-------|
| pli_004 | 1 | 1860 Federal Census, Schuylkill Co., PA | FamilySearch (coll. 1473181) | S2 is on the tree but no q_001 assertions extracted; would name Thomas's wife (Patrick's mother) for the first time |
| pli_005 | 2 | **1870 Federal Census, Schuylkill Co., PA** | **Ancestry** (collection 7163) | Researcher-requested; Patrick ~25 may still be with Thomas; last census likely showing parents together |
| pli_006 | 3 | 1870 Federal Census, Schuylkill Co., PA | FamilySearch (coll. 1438024) | Fallback if Ancestry pli_005 yields nothing |
| pli_007 | 4 | 1880 Federal Census, Schuylkill Co., PA | FamilySearch (coll. 1417683) | Records relationship-to-head and both parents' birthplaces |
| pli_008 | 5 | Probate records, Schuylkill Co., PA, 1860–1900 | FamilySearch (browse) | Thomas's will or intestate estate naming Patrick as heir = direct parentage evidence |
| pli_009 | 6 | Church records (marriage), Schuylkill Co., PA, 1835–1850 | FamilySearch | Parents' marriage reveals mother's maiden name; corroborates Thomas as father |
| pli_010 | 7 | Church records (baptisms of siblings), Schuylkill Co., PA, 1845–1870 | FamilySearch | Siblings' baptisms name Thomas + wife as parents on a contemporaneous original record; also the required FAN item |
| pli_011 | 8 | 1900 Federal Census, Schuylkill Co., PA | FamilySearch (coll. 1325221) | Records parents' birthplaces for each person |
| pli_012 | 9 | Land / deed records, Schuylkill Co., PA, 1840–1880 | FamilySearch (browse) | Thomas as grantor/grantee; witnesses may be FAN members from the same Irish parish |

---

**Two important notes before executing:**

1. **Patrick's 1908 death certificate (S3)** is already in the project but has no parental-information assertions extracted for q_001. Pennsylvania certificates from 1906 onward carry fields for father's and mother's names — review S3 first.

2. **Patrick's Irish baptism** is inaccessible (parish of origin unknown). Siblings' baptisms in Schuylkill County Catholic parishes (pli_010) serve as the surrogate path.

---

**Execution routing:**
- **search-records** → pli_004, pli_006, pli_007, pli_008, pli_009, pli_010, pli_011, pli_012 (all FamilySearch)
- **search-external-sites** → pli_005 (Ancestry 1870 census)

The delegation did not authorize execution, so no searches have been launched automatically.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick was ~15 in 1860 and almost certainly still living with Thomas Flynn. The tree holds S2 (1860 census) as a quality-2 reference on the ParentChild relationship but the log shows no formal search and no parentage assertions for q_001 were extracted from it. The FamilySearch 'United States Census, 1860' (collection 1473181) is name-searchable. The 1860 household listing would identify Thomas's wife — Patrick's mother, who has no name anywhere in the project tree — and enumerate all children, corroborating Patrick's place in the family. Search variants: Flynn, Flyn, Flinn.

Specifically requested by the researcher. Ancestry's '1870 United States Federal Census' (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/) is name-searchable and covers this census year nationally. Patrick was ~25 in 1870 and may still be residing with Thomas or may have recently established his own household nearby. Thomas was ~52 if still living; his wife (Patrick's mother) may also appear. The 1870 census bridges the gap between the known household years and Patrick's independent adulthood, and could be the last census showing the parents together. Search variants: Flynn, Flyn, Flinn.

Fallback for pli_002: if the Ancestry 1870 census search yields no clear result, the same federal enumeration is accessible via FamilySearch 'United States Census, 1870' (collection 1438024), which is name-searchable. Searches an independent index of the identical original enumeration and may resolve transcription variants that Ancestry missed.

The 1880 census is uniquely valuable for parentage: it records each person's stated relationship to the head of household and the birthplaces of both parents as discrete fields. Patrick was ~35 in 1880 and likely heads his own household; the enumeration would record his parents' birthplaces even if both were deceased by then. If Thomas was still living (~62), his separate household would name his wife alongside him. Searching for both Thomas Flynn's and Patrick Flynn's Schuylkill County households. FamilySearch 'United States Census, 1880' (collection 1417683) is name-searchable. Search variants: Flynn, Flyn, Flinn.

Thomas Flynn born ~1818; assuming he lived to age 42-82, his death and any probate would fall roughly 1860-1900 — this item's date window is bounded by Thomas's plausible lifespan. S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is already in the project tree as a source but has no assertions extracted for q_001. The FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); county volume 007936749 (Probate Records 1851-1930) is also browse-only (personCount 0). Browse image-by-image through the Schuylkill County dockets in this period. A will naming Patrick Flynn as Thomas's son would be direct parentage evidence; an intestate administration naming heirs would serve equally. The loc_001 entry confirms the Register of Wills has held probate records since 1811.

Dedicated search for the parents' marriage to each other — required for a parentage plan. Thomas Flynn likely married before 1845 (Patrick's birth year); for Irish Catholic immigrants in the Schuylkill County anthracite region, the Catholic parish register is the near-universal marriage source. The FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount 982,415) and covers 1708-1985. The marriage record supplies the mother's maiden name and, by its date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth, corroborates Thomas as Patrick's father — though the marriage alone does not prove Patrick is their child; a record placing him with the couple is still needed. Note: the surname this record gives her may be a prior married name if this was not her first marriage, but no earlier marriage for Thomas's wife is currently known or suspected. Search variants: Flynn, Flyn, Flinn.

Patrick was born ~1845 in Ireland (per the 1850 census) and his Irish baptism is inaccessible because the parish of origin is unknown. However, any siblings born in the US after the family's arrival would have been baptized in a Schuylkill County Catholic parish, and those records name Thomas and his wife as parents — providing contemporaneous original evidence of Thomas's paternity on a different document. The same name-searchable collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH covers this range; volume 007936751 (Church Records 1842-1895, personCount 0) is a browse-only fallback for records not yet in the index. Searching under Flynn (variants: Flyn, Flinn) for any baptism in Thomas's household. This item also serves as the required FAN item: each sibling's baptism names the parents and thereby directly bears on the subject's parentage.

Patrick was ~55 in 1900 and would head his own household. Thomas is certainly deceased by this point (he would be ~82). The 1900 census records each person's parents' birthplaces; Patrick's household entry would confirm his parents' countries of birth (Ireland for both, per the tree's working hypothesis) and corroborate the narrative across the full research window. For women enumerated, the 1900 schedule also records years married and children born vs. living — relevant if Patrick's wife appears. Covers the later half of the research window before Patrick's 1908 death. FamilySearch 'United States Census, 1900' (collection 1325221) is name-searchable. Search variants: Flynn, Flyn, Flinn.

Land deeds name the grantor, grantee, and witnesses — who are FAN members (neighbors and associates), frequently emigrants from the same Irish parish as the party. Volume 007936752 (Deed Records 1815-1900) on FamilySearch is name-searchable (22% indexed); search Thomas Flynn as grantor or grantee and note all witnesses. Witnesses to Thomas's transactions could be identified as members of the same Irish community, supplying leads toward the family's county or parish of origin in Ireland — directly bearing on what records survive there. This item also establishes when Thomas was economically active in Schuylkill County, which constrains the window for the probate search in pli_005.

items.question: Besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, who were the other children of Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania; d. 1868, Greene County, Ohio) and his wife Sarah?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

entry.rationale: The 1850 federal census (collection 1401638, per loc_001) lists every household member by name, age, and birthplace. Thomas Hale and all children living at home in 1850 would appear — the five known children (Mary b. ~1836, John b. ~1838, Rebecca b. ~1841, William b. ~1844, Joseph b. ~1847) should be present alongside any additional children still at home. A child born after Joseph or before Mary would also appear if living in the household. This is the highest-probability single source for a complete mid-century family enumeration and is free on FamilySearch.

Thomas Hale died in 1868 in Greene County. His will or estate administration papers would enumerate all heirs, typically listing every child whether or not they lived locally. The locality entry (loc_001) confirms that Greene County probate records survive from 1803 and were held by the Greene County Probate Court after 1852 (collection 1992421 on FamilySearch). The date range extends through 1880 to capture delays in estate settlement. A will or intestate estate file naming all children is the most direct evidence for a complete enumeration, including any child who had left Ohio before 1870.

The 1860 federal census (collection 1473181, per loc_001) shows the household a decade after 1850. Children born between 1851 and 1860 would appear as infants or young children; older children who had left home by 1860 would appear in their own households. Comparing the 1860 and 1850 household lists reveals whether any new children arrived after Joseph (b. ~1847) and confirms which earlier children had moved out. Any child present in 1860 but absent from 1850 is an additional find.

Thomas died in 1868; by 1870 Sarah would be head of household with any remaining minor children. The 1870 federal census (collection 1438024, per loc_001) should be searched for Sarah Hale's household to identify children born in the late 1850s or early 1860s who were still minors in 1870. The 1870 census should also be searched for adult Hale children who had established their own households in Greene County, extending the family map beyond the parental home.

Ohio County Marriage records for Greene County (collection 1614804, per loc_001) should be searched for all Hale children marrying in this window. Marriage records in this collection often name the principals' parents; any entry listing Thomas Hale or Sarah Hale as parent would confirm or reveal an additional child. The five known children's individual marriage records should also be examined for siblings named as witnesses or bondsmen — a FAN-cluster check that can surface siblings not captured in household census listings. This item satisfies the enumerative question's marriage-coverage requirement and provides the plan's required FAN-directed search.

Children of Thomas and Sarah Hale who died before reaching adulthood would not appear in marriage records and may be absent from census household listings if they died between census years. FamilySearch holds Ohio death records from 1867 forward; Find A Grave and BillionGraves index Greene County cemeteries for deaths before and after that date. Any Hale child who died in infancy or childhood is a legitimate member of the complete enumeration even if absent from the probate — a grave marker or death entry establishes their existence and completes the death-records coverage required for this enumerative question.

Sarah Hale has no recorded death date and may still be living in 1880. The 1880 census includes a relationship-to-head column, making it especially useful: adult children living with or near Sarah would be identified as son or daughter in the relationship field. All Hale households in Greene County should be searched to map the family network at this date and identify any children not previously located in earlier censuses. A child who had migrated out of the county might be found in a neighboring county search using the same strategy.

The 1840 federal census lists household members by age/sex tally rather than by name, but it establishes how many children were in Thomas Hale's household before the named 1850 enumeration. If the 1840 entry shows children in age groups predating Mary (b. ~1836) — for example, a child aged 10-15 in 1840, born roughly 1825-1830 — that indicates older siblings not yet identified. The 1840 household sets the outer bound on the family's size early in the marriage and guides how far back to extend other searches.

If the FamilySearch census searches (items 1, 3, 4, 7, and 8) do not yield a clear household listing for Thomas or Sarah Hale due to transcription errors or alternate spellings, Ancestry.com holds the same federal census years with independent transcriptions that may surface entries the FamilySearch index misses. Variant spellings (Hale, Haile, Heale) should be tried. This fallback also covers the Greene County probate collection if FamilySearch's images are incomplete or the relevant volume is not yet digitized.

A search for original birth certificates for the Hale children is required by the enumerative question's breadth self-check. Ohio did not require statewide birth registration until 1867, and the children of Thomas and Sarah Hale were born approximately 1836 to the mid-1860s, before mandatory registration was in effect for nearly the entire birth window.

Create the first research plan for q_001 — besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, who were the other children of Thomas Hale and his wife Sarah?

projectPath: <workspace>

agent_returns.text:
Plan written successfully (pl_001, pli_001 through pli_010). The warnings are a schema note about locality scope and do not affect validity.

**Mode: Create — q_001** "Besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, who were the other children of Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania; d. 1868, Greene County, Ohio) and his wife Sarah?"

**Tree survey — facts already recorded:**
- Thomas Hale (I1): birth ~1810, Pennsylvania; death 1868, Greene County, Ohio. No sources attached.
- Sarah Hale (I2): no dates or facts of any kind recorded. No sources attached.
- Mary (I3): birth ~1836, Greene County, Ohio. No sources.
- John (I4): birth ~1838, Greene County, Ohio. No sources.
- Rebecca (I5): birth ~1841, Greene County, Ohio. No sources.
- William (I6): birth ~1844, Greene County, Ohio. No sources.
- Joseph (I7): birth ~1847, Greene County, Ohio. No sources.

No fact on any person is sourced; all starting-point information is unsupported assumption or unverified family data. The locality entry (loc_001) supplies the collections and the key quirk: Greene County probate records survive from 1803, held by the Greene County Probate Court after 1852.

**Plan pl_001 — 9 planned items + 1 skipped, in execution order:**

- **pli_001** — census, Greene County, Ohio, 1850, FamilySearch — the 1850 federal census (collection 1401638) names every household member; highest-probability single source to enumerate all children at home at mid-century, including any born before Mary or after Joseph
- **pli_002** — probate, Greene County, Ohio, 1868-1880, FamilySearch — Thomas's will or estate administration (collection 1992421) would directly list all heirs, including children who had left Ohio; the most complete single enumeration of all children possible
- **pli_003** — census, Greene County, Ohio, 1860, FamilySearch — the 1860 census (collection 1473181) reveals children born after 1850 and shows which older children had left the parental home
- **pli_004** — census, Greene County, Ohio, 1870, FamilySearch — Thomas died 1868; Sarah would be head of household with any late-born minor children; also searches adult Hale households formed in Greene County by 1870 (collection 1438024)
- **pli_005** — vital_record (marriage), Greene County, Ohio, 1855-1890, FamilySearch — marriage records (collection 1614804) name parents and show siblings as witnesses or bondsmen; the FAN-cluster check on the complete sibling set; satisfies the marriage coverage requirement
- **pli_006** — cemetery, Greene County, Ohio, 1836-1900, FamilySearch — Ohio death records from 1867 forward plus Find A Grave / BillionGraves for Greene County cemeteries; covers children who died before adulthood and never appear in marriage or surviving census records; satisfies the death coverage requirement
- **pli_007** — census, Greene County, Ohio, 1880, FamilySearch — relationship-to-head column identifies sons/daughters in extended households; Sarah may still be living; adult children who left by 1870 may be findable here in their own Greene County households
- **pli_008** — census, Greene County, Ohio, 1840, FamilySearch — age/sex tallies only (no names in 1840), but establishes whether any children pre-date Mary (~1836) and sets the outer bound on the family's size early in the marriage
- **pli_009** — census, Greene County, Ohio, 1840-1880, Ancestry — fallback for pli_001: independent transcriptions on Ancestry may recover Hale entries missed by FamilySearch due to spelling variation (Hale, Haile, Heale); also covers probate if FamilySearch images are incomplete
- **pli_010** — vital_record, Ohio, 1836-1867, FamilySearch — SKIPPED (no_coverage): Ohio statewide birth registration did not begin until 1867; the Hale children's births fall almost entirely before this date; birth evidence will come from census, church, and probate records instead

**Enumerative breadth self-check:** Birth (pli_010, skipped with reason), Marriage (pli_005), Death (pli_006), Census (pli_001, 003, 004, 007, 008), Probate (pli_002) — all five event types are covered or formally skipped. FAN item satisfied by pli_005 (witnesses in known children's marriage records).

**Hand-back:** search-records for pli_001 through pli_008 (FamilySearch items) and search-external-sites for pli_009 (Ancestry). The delegation did not authorize execution.

---

This plan targets the question of whether Thomas and Sarah Hale of Greene County, Ohio had any children beyond the five already known. It works outward from the two richest sources — the 1850 federal census, which would name every person in the household, and Thomas's 1868 probate estate, which would list all his heirs — then cross-checks with the 1860, 1870, 1840, and 1880 censuses to catch children born at different points in the marriage and those who had left home before any single census year. Marriage records for all Hale children in the county are searched next, both to confirm the known five and to find any additional child who married but never appeared in the parental household at a census date. Cemetery and death records complete the picture by accounting for children who died before adulthood and would otherwise be invisible to every other search. If any FamilySearch entry proves hard to find due to spelling variation, Ancestry provides a fallback with its own independent transcriptions.

Would you like me to start executing this plan? The first step would be searching the 1850 federal census for Thomas Hale's household in Greene County, Ohio on FamilySearch.

items.rationale: The 1850 federal census (collection 1401638, per loc_001) lists every household member by name, age, and birthplace. Thomas Hale and all children living at home in 1850 would appear — the five known children (Mary b. ~1836, John b. ~1838, Rebecca b. ~1841, William b. ~1844, Joseph b. ~1847) should be present alongside any additional children still at home. A child born after Joseph or before Mary would also appear if living in the household. This is the highest-probability single source for a complete mid-century family enumeration and is free on FamilySearch.

Thomas Hale died in 1868 in Greene County. His will or estate administration papers would enumerate all heirs, typically listing every child whether or not they lived locally. The locality entry (loc_001) confirms that Greene County probate records survive from 1803 and were held by the Greene County Probate Court after 1852 (collection 1992421 on FamilySearch). The date range extends through 1880 to capture delays in estate settlement. A will or intestate estate file naming all children is the most direct evidence for a complete enumeration, including any child who had left Ohio before 1870.

The 1860 federal census (collection 1473181, per loc_001) shows the household a decade after 1850. Children born between 1851 and 1860 would appear as infants or young children; older children who had left home by 1860 would appear in their own households. Comparing the 1860 and 1850 household lists reveals whether any new children arrived after Joseph (b. ~1847) and confirms which earlier children had moved out. Any child present in 1860 but absent from 1850 is an additional find.

Thomas died in 1868; by 1870 Sarah would be head of household with any remaining minor children. The 1870 federal census (collection 1438024, per loc_001) should be searched for Sarah Hale's household to identify children born in the late 1850s or early 1860s who were still minors in 1870. The 1870 census should also be searched for adult Hale children who had established their own households in Greene County, extending the family map beyond the parental home.

Ohio County Marriage records for Greene County (collection 1614804, per loc_001) should be searched for all Hale children marrying in this window. Marriage records in this collection often name the principals' parents; any entry listing Thomas Hale or Sarah Hale as parent would confirm or reveal an additional child. The five known children's individual marriage records should also be examined for siblings named as witnesses or bondsmen — a FAN-cluster check that can surface siblings not captured in household census listings. This item satisfies the enumerative question's marriage-coverage requirement and provides the plan's required FAN-directed search.

Children of Thomas and Sarah Hale who died before reaching adulthood would not appear in marriage records and may be absent from census household listings if they died between census years. FamilySearch holds Ohio death records from 1867 forward; Find A Grave and BillionGraves index Greene County cemeteries for deaths before and after that date. Any Hale child who died in infancy or childhood is a legitimate member of the complete enumeration even if absent from the probate — a grave marker or death entry establishes their existence and completes the death-records coverage required for this enumerative question.

Sarah Hale has no recorded death date and may still be living in 1880. The 1880 census includes a relationship-to-head column, making it especially useful: adult children living with or near Sarah would be identified as son or daughter in the relationship field. All Hale households in Greene County should be searched to map the family network at this date and identify any children not previously located in earlier censuses. A child who had migrated out of the county might be found in a neighboring county search using the same strategy.

The 1840 federal census lists household members by age/sex tally rather than by name, but it establishes how many children were in Thomas Hale's household before the named 1850 enumeration. If the 1840 entry shows children in age groups predating Mary (b. ~1836) — for example, a child aged 10-15 in 1840, born roughly 1825-1830 — that indicates older siblings not yet identified. The 1840 household sets the outer bound on the family's size early in the marriage and guides how far back to extend other searches.

If the FamilySearch census searches (items 1, 3, 4, 7, and 8) do not yield a clear household listing for Thomas or Sarah Hale due to transcription errors or alternate spellings, Ancestry.com holds the same federal census years with independent transcriptions that may surface entries the FamilySearch index misses. Variant spellings (Hale, Haile, Heale) should be tried. This fallback also covers the Greene County probate collection if FamilySearch's images are incomplete or the relevant volume is not yet digitized.

A search for original birth certificates for the Hale children is required by the enumerative question's breadth self-check. Ohio did not require statewide birth registration until 1867, and the children of Thomas and Sarah Hale were born approximately 1836 to the mid-1860s, before mandatory registration was in effect for nearly the entire birth window.
items.skip_reason: Ohio statewide birth registration did not begin until 1867; the Hale children's births fall almost entirely before this date, leaving no meaningful birth certificate collection covering this population for this period. Birth evidence will instead come from census, church, and probate records.

**Plan pl_001 written for q_001 — Who were the parents of Katharina Seeger (b. c. 1843, Baiersbronn)?**

---

**What you need to do — 5 steps, all at Archion:**

Since FamilySearch holds nothing for Baiersbronn, every search runs through **Archion** (paid German church-archive portal). Start here:
👉 https://www.archion.de/de/alle-archive/baden-wuerttemberg/evangelisches-archiv-baden-und-wuerttemberg-wuerttemberg/dekanat-freudenstadt/baiersbronn

---

**Step 1 — pli_001 | Familienregister**
Browse the *Familienregister* (consolidated household register) for **Seeger** family entries. This is the most efficient starting point — it lists the father, mother's maiden name, and all children in one place.

**Step 2 — pli_002 | Baptism register, 1840–1846**
Browse baptism records for Katharina's own baptism entry, which directly names both parents. Also check spellings *Seger* and *Säger*.

**Step 3 — pli_003 | Marriage register, 1810–1843**
Browse for the parents' marriage entry to confirm the couple and obtain the mother's maiden name.

**Step 4 — pli_004 | Baptism register, 1815–1870 (siblings)**
Browse for siblings who name the same Seeger father — each sibling baptism independently names both parents, providing corroborating evidence.

**Step 5 — pli_005 | Burial/death record**
Browse the burial register (pre-1870, Archion) or obtain a civil death certificate (post-1870, Landesarchiv) for Katharina's death entry, which may state her age, birthplace, and parents' names.

---

**Next action:** Open Archion, start with the Familienregister, and browse for Seeger entries. If you capture a page image and upload it, I can help record the findings.

entry.rationale: The Familienregister is the most efficient record type for a parentage question in Württemberg. Baiersbronn's Protestant church maintained this consolidated register listing each family unit — father, mother with maiden name, and all children with birth dates and annotations. Browsing for Seeger family entries will directly link Katharina to her parents in a single record rather than piecing together separate annual registers. The loc_001 locality entry confirms that all Baiersbronn Protestant registers, including the Familienregister, are held on Archion (paid), not on FamilySearch; collections_search and volume_search returned nothing for this place, confirming no FamilySearch alternative exists.

Katharina's own baptism entry (~1843) in the Baiersbronn Protestant baptism register is the primary direct evidence for her parents: it names the father and the mother with her maiden name. The loc_001 locality entry places this register on Archion (paid); FamilySearch has no collections or digitised volumes for this place, so this is a browse of the annual baptism register for 1840–1846. When browsing, also check name variants 'Seger' and 'Säger' in case the clerk used an alternate spelling.

A dedicated search for the parents' marriage is required for any parentage question. The Baiersbronn Protestant marriage register (Archion, browse-only) will confirm the father and mother as a couple and supply the mother's maiden name, which later census and death records rarely include. The marriage date, placed before Katharina's birth (~1843), corroborates parentage evidence from the baptism and Familienregister. Caution: the couple's marriage proves they married but does not by itself establish that Katharina is their child — that link requires the baptism or Familienregister placing her with them. Date range sized to the years a parent of a child born in 1843 could plausibly have married.

A parentage question requires at least one FAN item. Browsing the Baiersbronn baptism register across the siblings' likely birth years for other children naming the same Seeger father will confirm the family unit and may name additional children who themselves name both parents. Each sibling's baptism entry independently names the same father and mother, building confidence in the parentage conclusion and providing cross-references if any single entry is damaged or unclear. Date range sized to the years a couple who married before 1843 could plausibly have had children.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: The 1880 U.S. Census is the first federal census to record each person's relationship to the head of household and each person's parents' birthplaces. Patrick Flynn (~35 in 1880) likely heads his own household; the record would show his relationship to any co-resident Thomas Flynn and would independently report Patrick's parents' birthplaces (Ireland). The locality guide (loc_001) notes PA civil registration did not start until 1906, so this census is a key pre-certificate source. Name-searchable (personCount 50,169,452). This is the highest-probability single record for simultaneously confirming co-residence and parents' origins.

The 1900 U.S. Census asks each person's birthplace and their father's and mother's birthplaces, and records the number of years in the United States. Patrick Flynn (~55 in 1900) should appear; the record corroborates or refines the Ireland birthplace and may give a county of origin, narrowing the Irish baptism search. Name-searchable (personCount 76,211,837). Patrick died 1908-03-12, so 1900 is the last decennial census in which he appears.

The 1860 U.S. Census is already cited on the ParentChild relationship (tree source S2) but no assertions have been extracted from it for q_001. Searching it directly confirms Patrick (~15) in Thomas's household and may reveal other household members — a wife or other children — not yet documented. A woman co-residing under the same surname, or children sharing the household, would help establish the family unit and potentially name the mother. Name-searchable (personCount 27,518,891).

The 1870 U.S. Census covers the period when Patrick (~25) may still be in Thomas's household or recently launched independently. Thomas (~52) would still be alive. Finding both in the same 1870 household is additional co-residence evidence and may show younger siblings or a wife for Thomas whose name has not yet been identified. Name-searchable (personCount 38,558,371).

Ancestry's 1870 United States Federal Census (collection 7163) is a separate index from FamilySearch's and is searched when the FamilySearch index returns nothing — different transcriptions may render an Irish surname differently. Paid collection. Searched only if pli_004 (FamilySearch 1870) yields nothing.

Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 Ireland) plausibly died between 1860 and 1900 (ages 42-82); the date range is set to Thomas's plausible lifespan, not Patrick's research window. The project tree already lists Schuylkill County Probate Records (S4) as a source, but no assertions from it have been extracted for q_001. A will naming Patrick as a son would be direct evidence of parentage. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (FamilySearch, 1683-1994) is browse-only (personCount 0); image group 007936749 (Schuylkill County Probate Records, 1851-1930) is also browse-only (personCount 0) — browse both image-by-image for Flynn entries in the target range. The locality guide (loc_001) confirms probate records are held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills, available from 1811.

Baptism records of Patrick's siblings in Schuylkill County would name both Thomas Flynn and his wife (Patrick's mother), whose name is entirely unknown in the project tree. The locality guide (loc_001) notes RC parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (Allentown from 1961); sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable (personCount 982,415), covering 1708-1985. Search for children baptized to Thomas Flynn (and variant spellings) between 1840 and 1870 — siblings born before 1845 Ireland or after arrival in Pennsylvania. A sibling's baptism entry naming both parents is corroborating evidence for Patrick's parentage and supplies the mother's name for further searches. This is a FAN-cluster item: the siblings are the associates whose records bear on the subject.

If the indexed church records search (pli_007) returns nothing — possible because the locality guide (loc_001) warns that some anthracite-region church films are browse-only — browse image group 007936751 (Schuylkill County Church Records, 1842-1895) image-by-image for Flynn entries. This volume is browse-only (personCount 0). Searched only if pli_007 yields no sibling baptism naming Thomas Flynn and a wife.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage record may name his father (Thomas Flynn) in the groom's-father field, which was common in Pennsylvania county marriage bonds and certificates of the period. Patrick was born ~1845 and would plausibly have married between 1865 and 1895. Image group 007936753 (Schuylkill County Marriage Records, 1870-1910) is browse-only (personCount 0) — browse image-by-image for Patrick Flynn entries. A marriage entry naming Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father would be additional corroborating evidence from a different record type.

Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 Ireland) would have naturalized in Pennsylvania after arrival. He appears in Schuylkill County by 1850, so he likely filed a declaration of intention or a petition for naturalization in Schuylkill County between 1849 and 1860. Naturalization petitions of this period sometimes list family members, including children and their ages, which would directly name Patrick as a son. Image group 007936750 (Schuylkill County Naturalization Records, 1849-1915) is browse-only (personCount 0) — browse image-by-image for Thomas Flynn entries. This is a FAN-cluster item: Thomas's own naturalization record bears on identifying Patrick's parentage.

Patrick Flynn was born ~1845 and would have been aged 16-20 during the Civil War (1861-1865), making him eligible for enlistment. The United States, Civil War Soldiers Index (FamilySearch, personCount 6,282,360) is name-searchable. If Patrick appears, a subsequent search of his compiled service record or pension application at NARA may yield parental information — pension files often include affidavits from family members naming parents, especially for minors at enlistment. This is a contingency item: searched to test whether Patrick served and whether his service record holds parentage evidence.

A dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife (Patrick's mother, name unknown) is required for a parentage question: the couple's marriage record supplies the mother's maiden name and corroborates Thomas as the father named by indirect and derivative evidence (census co-residence, death certificate). Patrick was born in Ireland ~1845, meaning this marriage predated emigration and took place in Ireland, likely between 1835 and 1845. Thomas was born ~1818, so he would have been aged 17-27 in that window. NOTE: An Ireland locality guide is not present in the project's localities section. This item cannot be properly planned or executed until the orchestrator commissions a locality guide for Ireland. The item is written here to mark the gap required by Standard 14. Date range is set to Thomas Flynn's plausible marriage window, not Patrick's research window in Pennsylvania.

Plan written successfully. Here is the full return.

**Mode:** create — first plan for q_001 "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Step 1 survey — facts already recorded that bear on the question:**
- Patrick Flynn (I1): Birth ~1845, Ireland (from 1850 census, F1); Death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County PA (from death cert S3, F2)
- Thomas Flynn (I2): Birth ~1818, Ireland — candidate father; no source is cited for this birth fact in the tree
- R1 (Thomas→Patrick, ParentChild): cited on 1850 census (S1), 1860 census (S2), and death cert (S3), all at quality 2 (inferred/secondary)
- Only two assertions exist for q_001 (a_004, a_005): both from the 1850 census, both about household position only; the parental-name fields of S3 (1908 death certificate) and S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) have not been extracted
- No mother is documented anywhere in the project tree
- Patrick has no spouse or children recorded in the tree
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) appears as a gedcomx source but produced zero assertions

**Extraction gap (flag before executing the plan):** The 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (S3) is already in the project tree and cited on the ParentChild relationship, but no assertions naming Patrick's father or mother have been extracted from it for q_001. Pennsylvania's 1906-onward death certificates carry a field for both parents' names. The extraction skill should review S3 before plan execution begins — it may immediately answer or narrow the question.

**Plan pl_002, 12 items:**

- pli_004 — census, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1880, FamilySearch — name-searchable; first census to record relationship to head and both parents' birthplaces; Patrick (~35) likely heads his own household; highest-probability item
- pli_005 — census, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1900, FamilySearch — name-searchable; records father's and mother's birthplaces; last decennial census Patrick can appear in (he died March 1908)
- pli_006 — census, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1860, FamilySearch — name-searchable; already cited as S2 on R1 but not extracted for q_001; may reveal other household members including Thomas's wife
- pli_007 — census, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1870, FamilySearch — name-searchable; may still show Patrick in Thomas's household or document Thomas's wife for the first time
- pli_008 — census, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1870, Ancestry — fallback for pli_007; independent 1870 transcription (collection 7163: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/); searched only if pli_007 yields nothing
- pli_009 — probate, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1860-1900, FamilySearch — browse-only (personCount 0); date range set to Thomas Flynn's plausible lifespan (born ~1818, plausibly died age 42-82), not Patrick's window; tree source S4 already listed but not extracted; a will naming Patrick as son is direct parentage evidence; browse image group 007936749
- pli_010 — church, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1842-1895, FamilySearch — name-searchable (personCount 982,415); sibling baptisms naming Thomas Flynn and wife supply the mother's name, which is entirely absent from the tree; FAN-cluster item
- pli_011 — church, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1842-1895, FamilySearch — browse-only (personCount 0), fallback for pli_010; browse image group 007936751 (English and German); triggered by loc_001 quirk that some anthracite-region church films are browse-only
- pli_012 — vital_record, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1865-1895, FamilySearch — browse-only (personCount 0); Patrick's own marriage record may name Thomas Flynn as groom's father; browse image group 007936753
- pli_013 — court, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1849-1875, FamilySearch — browse-only (personCount 0); Thomas Flynn's naturalization petition may list family members including Patrick by name; browse image group 007936750; FAN-cluster item
- pli_014 — military, United States, 1861-1865, FamilySearch — name-searchable (personCount 6,282,360); Patrick aged 16-20 during the Civil War; if found in the index, a pension application at NARA may carry parental affidavits
- pli_015 — church, Ireland, 1835-1848, repository TBD — required parentage item: the parents' marriage record supplies the mother's maiden name and corroborates Thomas as Patrick's father; BLOCKED — no Ireland locality guide is in the project; the orchestrator must commission locality-guide for Ireland before this item can be planned or executed

**Subject baptism / death-entry breadth check:** Patrick's baptism would be in Ireland (unknown parish), so it may not be accessible. The existing 1908 death certificate (S3) in the project tree covers the "subject's own death entry" requirement — but its parental-information fields have not been extracted (see extraction gap above).

**Hand-back:** search-records for pli_004 through pli_007, pli_009 through pli_011, pli_012 through pli_014 (all FamilySearch); search-external-sites for pli_008 (Ancestry, collection URL https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/); pli_015 is blocked pending an Ireland locality survey that the orchestrator should commission.

---

The question this plan addresses is who Patrick Flynn's parents were — a man born around 1845 in Ireland who spent his adult life and died in 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. The plan works through twelve searches in order of how likely each one is to name his parents directly. It starts with the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses, which are the first two that ask for a person's parents' birthplaces and relationship to the head of household, then revisits the 1860 and 1870 censuses where Patrick was likely still living near or with the candidate father Thomas Flynn. From there it turns to Thomas Flynn's probate records in Schuylkill County — a will naming Patrick as a son would settle the parentage question outright — followed by Schuylkill County church records searched for baptisms of Patrick's siblings, which would name both parents and reveal the mother whose name does not appear anywhere in the project yet. Patrick's own marriage record, Thomas's naturalization petition, and the Civil War soldiers index round out the Pennsylvania searches. The final item, a search for Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother in Ireland before the family emigrated, requires a separate research step for Irish records before it can be executed. Before any of these searches begin, the 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate already in the project should be reviewed: it almost certainly carries fields for Patrick's father's and mother's names, and extracting that information first may answer the question immediately.

Next, the FamilySearch items (the 1880 census first) will be searched, with the Ancestry 1870 census held in reserve as a fallback, and the Irish parents' marriage item waiting on a locality survey for Ireland.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

A Jöns Jönsson household entry in Västra Karaby or Barsebäck would record Elena's age, from which her birth year can be estimated; examiners sometimes noted that a person came from another parish. This plan targets the question of where Elena Asmundsdotter was born and who her parents were. Elena married Jöns Jönsson in Västra Karaby parish in December 1712, and her surname tells us her father's given name was Asmund — but nothing more about her origins is currently in the records. The plan opens with that known marriage event: first searching the national FamilySearch marriage index (which can be searched by name) for the 1712 entry, then browsing the original Västra Karaby parish register image directly to December 1712, since the original sometimes carries the bride's home parish or names her family witnesses. From there it searches the national baptism and burial indexes by name under all spelling variants of Elena, looking for her own birth record and her eventual burial (both of which commonly state an origin parish or age). A targeted browse of the Barsebäck parish register retrieves the 1718 christening of her son Asmund, whose entry names her as mother and may include her origin. Household examination books in the Västra Karaby volumes are browsed for an age entry on Elena. Two dedicated items pursue her parents: one searches the national marriage index for Asmund as a groom around 1680–1700 (to find Elena's mother's name), and one searches the national burial and baptism indexes for Asmund himself, sized to his plausible lifespan. The tax lists held at Riksarkivet cover the whole härad annually and would show an Asmund-headed household before Elena's marriage. Finally, Ancestry's separate indexing of the same Swedish marriage records serves as a fallback if the FamilySearch marriage index turns up nothing.

The next step is to run the name-searchable FamilySearch searches first — Elena's 1712 marriage, her baptism, her burial, the parents' marriage, and the father's records — then follow with the browse and external searches.

items.rationale: The 29 December 1712 marriage of Elena and Jöns Jönsson in Västra Karaby is the earliest anchored event in Elena's life. The national Sweden Marriages index (collection 1520596) is name-searchable. An index entry commonly records the bride's father's name—which Elena's patronymic 'Asmundsdotter' already establishes as Asmund—and may name her origin parish, directly answering the birthplace question. Search with variant given names noted on the Sweden Naming Customs wiki page: Elena, Helena, Elin, Ellen, Eljena, Lena; and patronymic abbreviations: Asmundsdotter, Asmundsd., Asmundsd. The locality quirk (loc_002) warns the national indexes are partial, so a negative result does not conclusively rule out the entry.

The Malmöhus Church Records collection (1974200) is browse-only (personCount 0) and holds the original Västra Karaby register volumes (image groups 004523018 and 004523021, covering from 1688, per loc_002). After the index search in item 1, browsing to December 1712 in the marriage register retrieves the original entry. The original may carry the bride's home parish, the names of witnesses (often kinsmen), or other details not preserved in the national index. This item is co-primary with item 1 rather than a fallback: the index reveals whether the record is indexed; the original image gives the full entry content regardless.

The national Sweden Baptisms index (collection 1520594) is name-searchable. Elena's birth year is estimated at roughly 1688–1700, based on her 1712 marriage at a presumed age of 12–24. The loc_002 quirk notes Västra Karaby's register begins 1688; if Elena was born before that date or in a different parish, no local entry will exist, making the national index the best first route to a birth record. Variant given names (Elena, Helena, Elin, Ellen, Eljena, Lena) and patronymic abbreviations (Asmundsdotter, Asmundsd.) must all be tried. A positive hit would directly name her birth parish and parents.

Elena's death date is unknown; her son Asmund's christening in September 1718 is the last documented presence. The national Sweden Burials index (collection 1520597) is name-searchable. A burial entry may state Elena's age—allowing back-calculation of her birth year—or name her home parish of origin. Per planning guidance, when a baptism may not exist because the birth may predate the local register (Västra Karaby's begins 1688, per loc_002) or fall in an unidentified parish, the subject's own burial entry is the standard alternative route to a birthplace. Date range sized to Elena's plausible lifespan after the 1718 son's christening.

Elena's son Asmund Jönsson was christened 11 September 1718 in Barsebäck—a known, date-pinned event in the project tree. Browsing to September 1718 in the Barsebäck register volumes (image groups 004514823 and 004514824, covering from 1648, per loc_001) within the browse-only (personCount 0) Malmöhus Church Records collection (1974200) retrieves the entry naming Elena as mother. Entries of this era sometimes spell out the mother's full patronymic or note her origin parish. This is a targeted browse, not a speculative one, and is one of the most efficient paths to a source naming Elena in her parental role.

Swedish husförhörslängder (household examination books) list all household members with their ages, updated at regular pastoral intervals. A Jöns Jönsson household entry in Västra Karaby or Barsebäck would record Elena's age, from which her birth year can be estimated; examiners sometimes noted that a person came from another parish. The Västra Karaby volumes in collection 1974200 (image group 004523018, coverage 1696-1720, per loc_002) are browse-only (personCount 0). Age evidence from the husförhör is essential if no indexed baptism is found in item 3, because it constrains the birth window and may identify the origin parish. ArkivDigital (https://www.arkivdigital.se/) holds additional digitized Swedish parish records and is an alternative browse path for these volumes.

A parentage question requires a dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other. Elena's father was named Asmund (established directly from her patronymic 'Asmundsdotter'). The national Sweden Marriages index (1520596) is name-searchable; searching for Asmund as a groom in Malmöhus area before approximately 1700 would identify Elena's mother—information that burial and census records typically omit. Date range is sized to Asmund's plausible role as Elena's father: if Elena was born ~1688–1700, her parents married most plausibly ~1678–1700. Note the limit: this marriage record confirms that this Asmund and wife wed, but it is not by itself evidence that Elena is their child; that link requires a record that places Elena with these parents (her baptism, a husförhör, or a probate naming her).

Elena's patronymic 'Asmundsdotter' establishes her father's given name as Asmund. This FAN-directed item searches the national Sweden Burials index (1520597) — name-searchable — for Asmund dying in Malmöhus area, and the national Baptisms index (1520594) for Asmund born in Malmöhus area. A burial entry for Asmund may state the parish where he lived, name survivors (including Elena), or give his age; his own baptism would show his parents and the parish the family originated from. Both records bound his lifespan as Elena's father: born approximately 1645–1665, died approximately 1680–1730. Date range sized to Asmund's lifespan as the creator of these records, not to Elena's research window. The loc_002 quirk states that household tax lists (mantalslängder) survive for the härad from 1658 and are held at Riksarkivet. The external collections search this session confirmed Riksarkivet's Mantalslängder portal covers 1642–1820 (https://sok.riksarkivet.se/mantalslangder). These annual household lists name household members by name and gender, including unmarried daughters resident in the household. A household headed by a man named Asmund in Harjager härad before Elena's 1712 marriage would place her in that household and identify her birth parish. Date range sized to Elena's pre-marriage years and her father's plausible lifespan as the household head.

The external collections search this session returned 'Sweden Select Marriages, 1630-1920' at Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/60363). - FS source SD-KER-BAP (baptism, 1842): names father Patrick Kerrigan, mother Mary Gallagher, sponsors John Gallagher and Bridget Kerrigan — direct parentage evidence.
- FS source SD-KER-1850 (1850 census): Patrick Kerrigan household, Pottsville — Patrick 35, laborer, Ireland; Mary 32, Ireland; Thomas 8, Pennsylvania — corroborating co-residence.
- FamilySearch tree shows candidate father ZZKR-PA4 Patrick Kerrigan, born ~1815 County Mayo, died 1880 Pottsville; candidate mother ZZKR-MG5 Mary Gallagher, born ~1818 Ireland.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pli_001 | Church | Pottsville, Schuylkill County | 1842 | FamilySearch | 1842 baptism at St. Patrick's (source SD-KER-BAP) names Patrick Kerrigan and Mary Gallagher as parents — direct parentage evidence not yet in the project |

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Narrow before broad: specific county (Vigo, pli_002) follows broader state search (Ohio and Indiana, pli_001). The plan bridges the 1860 census to 1862 military service with military records (pli_003), filling the gap. Fallback logic is explicit: pli_008 (Ancestry 1860 census) is marked fallback_for pli_002 (FamilySearch 1860 census). Date ranges reach the later part of the window: the pension collection (1861-1934) extends well past 1865, capturing post-war household testimony. Tax lists (1848-1866) cover the full window including the end. No item waits on evidence only a later item can supply. The sequence is logically ordered from most accessible to least accessible sources.

dimensions.name: Jurisdiction accuracy
dimensions.rationale: Jurisdictions are correct for the time period. Vigo County, Indiana existed in 1818 and continues to present (per the locality's jurisdiction list). The plan correctly names Vigo County for 1860 and later items. The 1850 census item correctly searches both Ohio (Josiah's birth state) and Indiana, acknowledging he could have been in either at age 22. The military item correctly specifies Indiana for 1862-1865 service. The plan does not recommend searching in non-existent jurisdictions or miss historical boundary changes. The locality confirms Vigo County's continuous existence across the entire 1850-1865 window, and the plan respects this.
